concepts.name: Harshavardhana's Rise to Power and Dynasty
key_dimensions: Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty origin and capital Thanesar
Circumstances of accession — death of Rajyavardhana and abduction of Rajyashri by Deva Gupta of Malwa
Role of the Buddhist monk Divakaramitra in persuading Harsha to accept the throne
Shift of capital from Thanesar to Kanauj and its political significance

concepts.name: Harsha's Military Campaigns and the Limits of His Empire
key_dimensions: Five kingdoms brought under control — Punjab, Kannauj, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa
Defeat at the hands of Pulakesi II of Chalukyas on the Narmada river — significance as a check on southward expansion
Nature of empire: loose confederacy vs. centralized control — contrast with Gupta empire
UPSC trap: Harsha never controlled the Deccan; Narmada was the southern boundary

concepts.name: Primary Sources for Harsha's Reign: Harshacharita and Xuanzang's Si-Yu-Ki
key_dimensions: Harshacharita by Banabhatta — court biography, literary exaggeration vs. historical value
Xuanzang's (Hiuen Tsang) travelogue — Si-Yu-Ki as a complementary foreign account
Harsha's own literary works: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda — his identity as a playwright
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Banabhatta (Indian source) from Xuanzang (Chinese source) and their respective biases

concepts.name: Harsha's Administrative Structure: Central and Provincial Government
key_dimensions: King as the pivot — personal supervision of administration, described by Xuanzang
Council of ministers (Mantriparishad) and key officers: Mahasandhivigrahika (foreign minister), Mahabalasadhikrita (army chief)
Provincial divisions: Bhuktis → Vishayas → Gramas — similarity and contrast with Gupta system
UPSC trap: Harsha's administration was more feudatory and decentralized compared to the Mauryas, not a tight bureaucracy

concepts.name: Revenue System and Land Grants under Harsha
key_dimensions: State revenue divided into four parts: royal expenses, learned men, religious purposes, and officials/scholars
Heavy reliance on land grants (agrahara) to Brahmins and Buddhist monasteries — expansion of feudalism
Tax rate: Xuanzang mentions 1/6th of produce as revenue — comparatively mild
UPSC trap: Land grants weakened central authority by creating autonomous local powers — link to early medieval feudalism debate

concepts.name: Harsha's Army: Composition and Organization
key_dimensions: Four-fold army (Chaturanga): infantry, cavalry, chariots, elephants — elephants as most prized
Xuanzang's figures: 60,000 elephants, 100,000 cavalry — reliability and exaggeration question
Personal inspection of troops and camp — king's direct military involvement
Feudatory chiefs contributing forces — decentralized military command structure

concepts.name: Harsha's Religious Policy: Syncretism and Patronage
key_dimensions: Early life as a Shaiva; gradual conversion to Mahayana Buddhism under Xuanzang's influence
Continued patronage of Brahmins and Shaivism — policy of religious tolerance and syncretism
UPSC trap: Harsha was NOT an exclusive Buddhist; he patronized all three — Buddhism, Shaivism, and Brahminism
Persecution of an assassination plot by Brahmin opponents — indicates religious tensions despite tolerance

concepts.name: The Kanauj Assembly (643 CE): Organization and Significance
key_dimensions: Convened to honor Xuanzang and propagate Mahayana Buddhism
Duration: 23 days; attended by 20 kings, 1,000 Buddhist monks, 3,000 Brahmins and Jains
Harsha as patron — erected a 100-foot tall golden statue of the Buddha
UPSC trap: Kanauj Assembly is different from the Prayag (Allahabad) Assembly — do not conflate the two

concepts.name: The Prayag (Allahabad) Assembly (Quinquennial Assembly): Purpose and Charity
key_dimensions: Held every five years at the Triveni Sangam — Prayag
Harsha distributed all accumulated wealth to the poor, monks, and Brahmins — even gave away personal clothing
Described vividly by Xuanzang — 75-day festival of dana (charity)
UPSC trap: This was a regular welfare institution, not a one-time event; held every 5 years — contrast with Kanauj Assembly

concepts.name: Nalanda University under Harsha's Patronage
key_dimensions: Harsha as a major patron — grants of revenue from 100 villages for Nalanda's upkeep
Xuanzang as a student and later teacher at Nalanda — subjects taught: logic, grammar, metaphysics, Buddhism
Structure: 10,000 students, 1,500 teachers, 8-storey building described by Xuanzang
UPSC trap: Nalanda was founded earlier (Gupta period, possibly by Kumaragupta I) — Harsha patronized but did NOT found it

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Visit: Observations on Society, Economy, and Religion
key_dimensions: Observations on caste system, untouchability (butchers, fishermen, executioners living outside towns)
Economic life: use of cowrie shells as currency, decline of urban centers noted
Religious landscape: Buddhism in decline in some regions, Shaivism dominant in others
UPSC trap: Xuanzang's account reflects a mid-7th century snapshot — do not project it backward to the Gupta period

concepts.name: Harsha's Diplomatic Relations: Embassy to China
key_dimensions: Harsha sent an embassy to the Tang Emperor Taizong of China (643 CE) — first known diplomatic contact between India and China at state level
Chinese mission to India under Wang Xuance — political and cultural exchange
Significance: reflects Harsha's stature as a major power; evidence of India's international presence
UPSC trap: Wang Xuance's second visit after Harsha's death — he raised a Nepali-Tibetan army to defeat Harsha's usurper Arunasva

concepts.name: Condition of Buddhism During Harsha's Reign
key_dimensions: Mahayana Buddhism dominant in the north; Hinayana (Theravada) still present in the south and east
Decline indicators: many monasteries in ruins, monks reduced in number — as noted by Xuanzang
Harsha's personal role in reviving Buddhist institutions through dana and assemblies
UPSC trap: Buddhism was ALREADY in decline during Harsha's time — his patronage was a response to decline, not evidence of its flourishing

concepts.name: Mahayana vs. Hinayana Buddhism: Distinctions Relevant to Harsha's Period
key_dimensions: Mahayana: Bodhisattva ideal, idol worship, Sanskrit texts — preferred by Harsha and Xuanzang
Hinayana (Theravada): strict monastic code, Pali texts, no idol worship — dominant in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
Vajrayana emergence: tantric Buddhism developing in this period — early signs in Bengal/Bihar
UPSC trap: Xuanzang himself was a Mahayana scholar — his account is biased against Hinayana institutions

concepts.name: Post-Harsha Political Fragmentation and Its Administrative Causes
key_dimensions: Death of Harsha in 647 CE without an heir — rapid disintegration of empire
Feudatory chiefs (samanta system) reasserting independence — structural weakness of Harsha's empire
Rise of regional powers: Palas in Bengal, Gurjara-Pratiharas in the west — post-Harsha power vacuum
UPSC trap: The fragmentation was NOT sudden — it was built into the decentralized structure of Harsha's administration

concepts.name: The Samanta System: Feudatory Hierarchy under Harsha
key_dimensions: Samantas as subordinate kings paying tribute and providing military service — not salaried officials
Gradations: Maharaja, Mahasamanta, Samanta — hierarchy of feudatory lords
Link to early medieval feudalism: land grants + samanta system = weakening of centralized state
UPSC trap: The samanta system under Harsha is an early example of the feudalism debate (D.D. Kosambi vs. R.S. Sharma perspectives)

concepts.name: Harsha as a Playwright and Patron of Literature
key_dimensions: Three Sanskrit plays attributed to Harsha: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika (both comedies), Nagananda (Buddhist drama)
Nagananda unique — Buddhist theme of self-sacrifice (Jimutavahana's story); reflects Buddhist values
Patronage of Banabhatta (Harshacharita, Kadambari) — Kadambari considered first Sanskrit prose novel
UPSC trap: Do not confuse Harsha's own works with works written about him — Harshacharita is BY Banabhatta, not by Harsha

concepts.name: Condition of Women and Social Structure in Harsha's Period
key_dimensions: Xuanzang's observations: widow immolation (sati) practiced; women's education limited
Caste rigidity: untouchables (chandalas) segregated — lived outside city walls
Position of Buddhist nuns: presence in monasteries but subordinate to monks
UPSC trap: Social conditions described by Xuanzang represent the 7th century reality — do not generalize as 'Gupta-era' social norms

concepts.name: Economic Conditions During Harsha's Period: Trade and Urbanization
key_dimensions: Decline of long-distance trade compared to Gupta period — shrinkage of urban centers noted by Xuanzang
Cowrie shells as medium of exchange in some areas — indicates retreat from monetized economy
Agriculture as primary base; land grants creating self-sufficient rural units — link to feudal economy
UPSC trap: The economic decline was a structural shift, not a sudden collapse — connects to the broader early medieval economic debate

concepts.name: Harsha's Copper Plate Inscriptions and Epigraphic Evidence
key_dimensions: Madhuban Copper Plate and Banskhera Copper Plate — issued by Harsha, authenticated by his personal signature
Content: land grants, religious donations, administrative titles of officers
Significance: corroborate Xuanzang and Banabhatta accounts — triangulation of sources
UPSC trap: Harsha's inscriptions are FEW compared to Ashoka or Gupta kings — primary reliance is on literary sources, not epigraphy
